{{Short description|Special functions in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Painlevé transcendents''' are solutions to certain [[nonlinear differential equation|nonlinear]] [[second-order differential equation|second-order]] [[ordinary differential equation]]s in the complex plane with the '''Painlevé property''' (the only movable singularities are poles), but which are not generally solvable in terms of [[elementary function]]s. They were discovered by
{{harvs|txt|authorlink=Émile Picard|first=Émile|last=Picard|year=1889}},
{{harvs|txt|authorlink=Paul Painlevé|first=Paul |last=Painlevé|year=1900|year2=1902}},
{{harvs|txt|authorlink=:de:Richard Fuchs (Mathematiker)|first=Richard|last=Fuchs|year=1905}}, and
{{harvs|txt|authorlink=:de:Bertrand Gambier|first=Bertrand|last=Gambier|year=1910}}.

==History==

=== Origins ===
Painlevé transcendents have their origin in the study of [[special functions]], which often arise as solutions of differential equations, as well as in the study of [[isomonodromic deformation]]s of linear differential equations. One of the most useful classes of special functions are the [[elliptic function]]s. They are defined by second-order ordinary differential equations whose [[singularity (mathematics)|singularities]] have the '''Painlevé property''': the only [[movable singularity|movable singularities]] are [[pole (complex analysis)|poles]]. This property is rare in nonlinear equations.

Poincaré and [[Lazarus Fuchs]] showed that any first order equation (that is, an ODE involving only up to the first derivative) with the Painlevé property can be transformed into the [[Weierstrass elliptic function|Weierstrass elliptic equation]] or the [[Riccati equation#Complex analysis|Riccati equation]], all of which can be solved explicitly in terms of integration and previously known special functions.<ref>{{cite book | last=Conte | first=Robert | editor-first1=Robert | editor-last1=Conte |title=The Painlevé Property | publisher=Springer New York | publication-place=New York, NY | date=1999 | isbn=978-0-387-98888-7 | doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-1532-5|page=105}}</ref>

[[Émile Picard]] pointed out that for orders greater than 1, movable [[Essential singularity|essential singularities]] can occur, and found in {{harvs|txt|authorlink=|last=Picard|year=1889}} a special case of what was later called Painleve VI equation (see below). (For orders greater than 2 the solutions can have moving natural boundaries.) Specifically, let <math display="inline">\varphi</math> be the [[elliptic function]] defined by<math display="block">
\varphi: y \mapsto \varphi(y, x), \qquad y=\int_{\infty}^{\varphi} \frac{\mathrm{d} z}{\sqrt{z(z-1)(z-x)}}</math>
and let <math display="inline">\omega_1(x), \omega_2(x)</math> be its two half-periods. Then the function <math display="block">
u: x \mapsto u(x)=\varphi\left(2 c_1 \omega_1(x)+2 c_2 \omega_2(x), x\right)
</math>with <math display="inline">\left(c_1, c_2\right)</math> arbitrary constants satisfies the Painleve VI equation in the case of <math display="inline">\alpha=\beta=\gamma= \delta - 1/2 = 0</math>.<ref>{{Citation |last=Conte |first=R |chapter=The Painlevé methods |date=2019-04-23 |title=Classical and Quantum Nonlinear Integrable Systems |pages=39–126 |editor-last=Kundu |editor-first=A |chapter-url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/9781420034615/chapters/10.1201/9780429137891-2 |access-date=2025-03-30 |edition=1 |publisher=CRC Press |language=en |doi=10.1201/9780429137891-2 |isbn=978-0-429-13789-1 |last2=Musette‡ |first2=M|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Classification ===
Around 1900, [[Paul Painlevé]] studied second-order differential equations with no movable singularities. He found that up to certain transformations, every such equation of the form

:<math>y^{\prime\prime}=R(y^{\prime},y,t)</math>

(with <math>R</math> a [[rational function]]) can be put into one of 50 ''canonical forms'' (listed in {{harv|Ince|1956}}).

{{harvs|last=Painlevé|year1=1900|year2=1902|txt}} found that 44 of the 50 equations are reducible, in the sense that they can be solved in terms of previously known functions, leaving just 6 equations requiring the introduction of new special functions to solve them. These six second order nonlinear differential equations are called the Painlevé equations and their solutions are called the Painlevé transcendents. There were some computational errors, and as a result he missed 3 of the equations, including the general form of Painleve VI. Painlevé's student [[:de: Bertrand Gambier|Bertrand Gambier]] fixed the errors and completed the classification.

Independently of Painlevé and Gambier, equation Painleve VI was found by [[:de: Richard Fuchs|Richard Fuchs]] from completely different considerations: he studied [[isomonodromic deformation]]s of linear differential equations with [[regular singularities]].

The most general form of the sixth equation was missed by Painlevé, but was discovered in 1905 by Richard Fuchs (son of [[Lazarus Fuchs]]), as the differential equation satisfied by the singularity of a second order Fuchsian equation with 4 regular singular points on the [[projective line]] <math>\mathbf{P}^1</math> under [[isomonodromic deformation|monodromy-preserving deformations]]. It was added to Painlevé's list by {{harvs|txt|last=Gambier|year=1910}}.

=== Subsequent work ===
{{harvs|last=Chazy|year1=1910|year2=1911|txt}} tried to extend Painlevé's work to higher-order equations, finding some third-order equations with the Painlevé property.

It was an [[open problem]] for many years to show that these 6 equations really were irreducible for generic values of the parameters (they are sometimes reducible for special parameter values; see [[Painlevé transcendents#Special parameter values|below]]), but this was finally proved by {{harvtxt|Nishioka|1988}} and {{harvs|txt|last=Umemura|first= Hiroshi |year=1989}}.

==List of Painlevé equations==
{{multiple image | direction = vertical | width = 240 | footer = | image1 = PainleveTypeI.svg | alt1 = Painlevé transcendent of the first type | caption1 = | image2 = PainleveTypeII.svg | alt2 = Painlevé transcendent of the second type | caption2 = | image3 = PainleveTypeIII.svg | alt3 = Painlevé transcendent of the third type | caption3 = |}}

These six equations, traditionally called Painlevé I–VI, are as follows:
{{bulleted list

|1= I (Painlevé):

:<math>\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} = 6 y^2 +  t </math>

|2= II (Painlevé):

:<math>\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} = 2 y^3 + ty + \alpha </math>

|3= III (Painlevé):

:<math>\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} = 
\frac{1}{y}\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2-\frac{1}{t}\frac{dy}{dt} + \frac{1}{t}(\alpha y^2 + \beta) + \gamma y^3 + \frac{\delta}{y}</math>

|4= IV (Gambier):

:<math>\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}=\frac{1}{2y}\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2+\tfrac32y^3+4ty^2+2(t^2-\alpha)y+\frac{\beta}{y}</math>

|5= V (Gambier):

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}&=
\left(\frac{1}{2 y }+\frac{1}{ y -1}\right) \left( \frac{dy}{dt} \right)^2
-\frac{1}{t} \frac{dy}{dt}\\
&\quad+\frac{( y -1)^2}{t^2}\left(\alpha y +\frac{\beta}{ y }\right) +\gamma\frac{ y }{t}+\delta\frac{ y ( y +1)}{ y -1}\\
\end{align}</math>

|6= VI (Richard Fuchs):

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}&=
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{y-1}+\frac{1}{y-t}\right)\left( \frac{dy}{dt} \right)^2
-\left(\frac{1}{t}+\frac{1}{t-1}+\frac{1}{y-t}\right)\frac{dy}{dt} \\&\quad +
\frac{y(y-1)(y-t)}{t^2(t-1)^2}
\left\{\alpha+\beta\frac{t}{y^2}+\gamma\frac{t-1}{(y-1)^2}+\delta\frac{t(t-1)}{(y-t)^2}\right\}\\ 
\end{align}</math>

}}

The symbols <math>\alpha</math>, <math>\beta</math>, <math>\gamma</math>, <math>\delta</math> denote complex-valued constants.

If <math display="inline">\gamma \delta \neq 0</math> in <math display="inline">\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{III}}</math>, then one can set <math display="inline">\gamma=1</math> and <math display="inline">\delta=-1</math>, [[without loss of generality]], by rescaling <math display="inline">\alpha</math> and <math display="inline">\beta</math> if necessary. If <math display="inline">\gamma=0</math> and <math display="inline">\alpha \delta \neq 0</math> in <math display="inline">\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{III}}</math>, then set <math display="inline">\alpha=1</math> and <math display="inline">\delta=-1</math>, without loss of generality. Lastly, if <math display="inline">\delta=0</math> and <math display="inline">\beta \gamma \neq 0</math>, then one can set <math display="inline">\beta=-1</math> and <math display="inline">\gamma=1</math>, without loss of generality.

If <math display="inline">\delta \neq 0</math> in <math display="inline">\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{V}}</math>, then one can set <math display="inline">\delta=-\frac{1}{2}</math>, without loss of generality.<ref>[https://dlmf.nist.gov/32.2#ii NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §32.2(ii)]</ref>

==Singularities==

The singularities of solutions of these equations are 
*The point <math>\infty</math>, and
*The point 0 for types III, V and VI, and
*The point 1 for type VI, and
*Possibly some movable poles

For type I, the singularities are (movable) double poles of residue 0, and the solutions all have an infinite number of such poles in the complex plane. The functions with a double pole at <math>z_0</math> have the [[Laurent series]] expansion
:<math>(z-z_0)^{-2}-\frac{z_0}{10}(z-z_0)^2-\frac{1}{6}(z-z_0)^3+h(z-z_0)^4+\frac{z_0^2}{300}(z-z_0)^6+\cdots</math>
converging in some neighborhood of <math>z_0</math> (where <math>h</math> is some [[complex number]]). The location of the poles was described in detail by {{harvs|last=Boutroux|year1=1913|year2=1914}}. The number of poles in a ball of radius <math>R</math> grows roughly like a constant times <math>R^{5/2}</math>.

For type II, the singularities are all (movable) simple poles.

== Asymptotics ==

=== I ===
[[File:Painleve I with asymptotics.svg|thumb|Painlevé I solutions for <math display="inline">y(0)=0</math> and <math display="inline">y(0)=0</math>, for various values of <math>k</math>, with the asymptotic parabola.]]
There are solutions of Painlevé I such that<math display="block">
y(t)=-\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{6}|t|}+d|t|^{-1/8}\sin\left(\phi(t)-\theta_{0}\right)+o\left(|t|^{-1/8}\right)
</math>where<math display="block">
\phi(t)=(24)^{1/4}\left(\tfrac{4}{5}|t|^{5/4}-\tfrac{5}{8}d^{2}\ln|t|\right)
</math>and <math display="inline">d</math> and <math display="inline">\theta_{0}</math> are constants. There are also solutions such that <math display="block">
y(t)\sim\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{6}|t|}
</math>although such solutions are unstable under perturbation.

For given initial conditions <math display="inline">y(0)=0</math> and <math display="inline">y^{\prime}(0)=k</math>, with <math display="inline">k</math> real, <math display="inline">y(t)</math> has at least one pole on the real axis. There are two special values of <math display="inline">k</math>, <math display="inline">k_{1}</math> and <math display="inline">k_{2}</math>, with the properties <math display="inline">-0.451428<k_{1}<-0.451427</math>, <math display="inline">1.851853<k_{2}<1.851855</math>, such that if <math>k \in (k_1, k_2)</math> then the solution oscillates about, and is asymptotic to, <math>-\sqrt{|t|/6}</math>.<ref>[https://dlmf.nist.gov/32.11 NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions §32.11(i) First Painlevé Equation]</ref>

==Hamiltonian systems==
The Painlevé equations can all be represented as [[Hamiltonian system]]s.

Example: If we put
:<math>\displaystyle q=y,\quad p=y^{\prime}+y^2+t/2</math>
then the second Painlevé equation 
:<math>\displaystyle y^{\prime\prime} =2y^3+ty+b-1/2</math>
is equivalent to the Hamiltonian system
:<math>\displaystyle q^{\prime}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p} = p-q^2-t/2</math>
:<math>\displaystyle p^{\prime}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q} = 2pq+b</math>
for the Hamiltonian 
:<math>\displaystyle H=p(p-2q^2-t)/2 -bq.</math>

==Symmetries==
A [[Bäcklund transform]] is a transformation of the dependent and independent variables of a differential equation that transforms it to a similar equation. The Painlevé equations all have discrete groups of Bäcklund transformations acting on them, which can be used to generate new solutions from known ones.

===Example type I===

The set of solutions of the type I Painlevé equation 
:<math>y^{\prime\prime}=6y^2+t</math>
is acted on by the order 5 symmetry <math>y\to\zeta^3 y</math>, <math>t\to\zeta t</math> where <math>\zeta</math> is a fifth root of 1. There are two solutions invariant under this transformation, one with a pole of order 2 at 0, and the other with a zero of order 3 at 0.

===Example type II===

In the Hamiltonian formalism of the type II Painlevé equation
:<math>\displaystyle y^{\prime\prime}=2y^3+ty+b-1/2</math>
with 
:<math>\displaystyle q=y,p=y^\prime+y^2+t/2</math>
two Bäcklund transformations are given by
:<math>\displaystyle (q,p,b)\to (q+b/p,p,-b)</math>
and
:<math>\displaystyle (q,p,b)\to (-q, -p+2q^2+t,1-b).</math>
These both have order 2, and generate an [[infinite dihedral group]] of Bäcklund transformations (which is in fact the affine Weyl group of <math>A_1</math>; 
see below).
If <math>b=1/2</math> then the equation has the solution <math>y=0</math>; applying the Bäcklund transformations generates an infinite family of rational functions that are solutions, such as <math>y=1/t</math>, <math>y=2(t^3-2)/t(t^3-4)</math>, ...

Okamoto discovered that the [[parameter space]] of each Painlevé equation can be identified with the [[Cartan subalgebra]] of a [[semisimple Lie algebra]], such that actions of the [[affine Weyl group]] lift to Bäcklund transformations of the equations. The Lie algebras for 
<math>P_I</math>, <math>P_{II}</math>, <math>P_{III}</math>, <math>P_{IV}</math>, <math>P_V</math>, <math>P_{VI}</math> 
are 0, <math>A_1</math>, <math>A_1\oplus A_1</math>, <math>A_2</math>, <math>A_3</math>, and <math>D_4</math>.

== Special parameter values ==
<math>P_{\mathrm{I}}</math> has no free parameters. For the other cases, they are irreducible for generic parameter values, but for special parameter values they admit solutions that satisfy a first-order Riccati equation, which can be expressed in terms of special functions:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Clarkson |first=Peter A |date=April 2003 |title=Painlevé equations—nonlinear special functions |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0377042702005897 |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |language=en |volume=153 |issue=1-2 |pages=127–140 |doi=10.1016/S0377-0427(02)00589-7|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="DLMF32">{{cite web |title=Painlevé Transcendents |url=https://dlmf.nist.gov/32 |access-date=2026-03-28 |website=NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions}}</ref>

* rational solutions for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6;<ref>{{cite web |title=Rational Solutions |url=https://dlmf.nist.gov/32.8 |access-date=2026-03-28 |website=NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions}}</ref>
* algebraic solutions for 3, 5, 6;<ref>{{cite web |title=Other Elementary Solutions |url=https://dlmf.nist.gov/32.9 |access-date=2026-03-28 |website=NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions}}</ref>
* other special-function solutions: Airy for 2, Bessel for 3, parabolic-cylinder for 4, Whittaker for 5, and hypergeometric for 6.<ref>{{cite web |title=Special Function Solutions |website=NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions |url=https://dlmf.nist.gov/32.10 |access-date=2026-03-28}}</ref>

==Relation to other areas==

One of the main reasons Painlevé equations are studied is their relation with invariance of the [[monodromy]] of linear systems with [[regular singularities]] under changes in the locus of the poles. In particular, Painlevé VI was discovered by Richard Fuchs because of this relation. This subject is described in the article on [[isomonodromic deformation]].

The Painlevé equations are all reductions of integrable [[partial differential equation]]s; see {{harvs| last1=Ablowitz | first1=M. J. | last2=Clarkson | first2=P. A. | title=Solitons, nonlinear evolution equations and inverse scattering | publisher=Cambridge University Press | series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series | isbn=978-0-521-38730-9 | mr=1149378 | year=1991 | volume=149 | txt}}.

The Painlevé equations are all reductions of the [[self-dual Yang–Mills equations]]; see {{harvs|last1=Ablowitz|last2=Chakravarty|last3=Halburd|year=2003|txt}}.

The Painlevé transcendents appear in [[random matrix theory]] in the formula for the [[Tracy–Widom distribution]], the 2D [[Ising model]], the [[asymmetric simple exclusion process]] and in two-dimensional [[quantum gravity]].

<math>P_{\mathrm{II}}</math> has been used to describe a dynamic passage through a [[quantum phase transition]], leading to precise scaling of excitations and revealing relations to integrable multistate Landau-Zener models.<ref name='Itin-09pra'>{{cite journal|title=Dynamics of a many-particle Landau-Zener model|author1=A.P. Itin |author2=P. Torma |journal=[[Physical Review A]]|volume=79|issue=5|year=2007|article-number=055602|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.79.055602|arxiv=0902.3351}}</ref><ref name='Vijay-25NComm'>{{cite journal|title=Parametric tuning of quantum phase transitions in ultracold reactions|author1=V. G. Sadhasivam|author2=F. Suzuki|author3=B. Yan|author4=N. A. Sinitsyn|journal=[[Nature Communications]]|page=10246|year=2024|doi=10.1038/s41467-024-54489-3|doi-access=free|arxiv=2403.09291}}</ref> Integrable generalizations of <math>P_{\mathrm{II}}</math> have been found based on this application.<ref name='Tyagi-25pra'>{{cite journal|title=Asymmetry amplification by a nonadiabatic passage through a critical point|author1=B. Tyagi|author2=F. Suzuki|author3=V. Y. Chernyak|author4=N. A. Sinitsyn |journal=[[Physical Review A]]|volume=111|year=2025|article-number=032205|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.111.032205|arxiv=2408.15897}}</ref>

<math>P_{\mathrm{VI}}</math> appears in [[two-dimensional conformal field theory]]: it is obeyed by combinations of [[Virasoro conformal block|conformal blocks]] at both <math>c=1</math> and <math>c=\infty</math>, where <math>c</math> is the [[central charge]] of the [[Virasoro algebra]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gamayun |first=O. |last2=Iorgov |first2=N. |last3=Lisovyy |first3=O. |date=2012-10-04 |title=Conformal field theory of Painlevé VI |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/JHEP10(2012)038 |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |language=en |volume=2012 |issue=10 |pages=38 |doi=10.1007/JHEP10(2012)038 |issn=1029-8479|arxiv=1207.0787 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Litvinov |first=Alexey |last2=Lukyanov |first2=Sergei |last3=Nekrasov |first3=Nikita |last4=Zamolodchikov |first4=Alexander |date=2014-07-29 |title=Classical conformal blocks and Painlevé VI |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/JHEP07(2014)144 |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |language=en |volume=2014 |issue=7 |pages=144 |doi=10.1007/JHEP07(2014)144 |issn=1029-8479|arxiv=1309.4700 }}</ref>
